master_narrator.agency_handoff_prompt:
Isla didn't trust hard drives. They spun. They failed. They rusted. Crystals were forever. 

She adjusted the thirty-second brass Helmholtz Vernier ring, her movements economical and tight. In the center of the darkened Simulacrum chamber, a fingernail-sized quartz lattice drank violet laser light. Around it, suspended entirely by magneto-acoustic cymatics, droplets of liquid iron orbited in a gravity-defying dance, keeping time to a minor-key cello chord played by a polyphonic synthesizer.

She was encoding terabytes per second of five-dimensional holographic storm telemetry into the nanostructured quartz. It was a staggering feat of computational architecture. Yet, here she was, pausing every four minutes to hand-polish the primary optical lenses with a scrap of chamois leather until her fingers cramped. 

"If you're complaining and no one is laughing, you're complaining wrong," Isla muttered to herself, snapping the chamois crisp. She checked the acoustic tables. Orion's cymatic intuition was ninety-four percent accurate, which would be infuriating if the remaining six percent didn't require her boundary tensors to keep the ferrofluid from splashing onto the ceiling.

The synthesizer hit a low, resonant note, and the ferrofluid spires spiked in perfect synchronization. She exhaled, a sharp, controlled breath. The lattice was stable. Now, she just needed to hand off the telemetry logs to Dorian before the chronicler started weaving wild tales about 'iron elementals' in the dark.

She picked up the brass-bound slate, wiping a microscopic speck of dust from the screen, and stepped out into the humming corridor to find him.
